 Wise Wife Ground Cinnamon Recalled in 14 States After Connecticut Lab Finds Elevated Lead
 Published Nov 01, 2026 9:45 PM EST 
 By
 Dorothy Brooks 
 Ruby Sengar | Pexels 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 A New York spice distributor is recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon sold in 14 states after a Connecticut state laboratory found elevated levels of lead in a sample. SLR Food Distribution Inc. of Hicksville, New York, announced the voluntary recall Oct. 29, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration posted the company's recall notice the same day.
 The recalled product comes in a 110-gram (3.88-ounce) clear plastic container with a black screw-top cap. It carries UPC 0688474302754 on the back label and a "Best Before" date of 4/25/2027. The company said it shipped the cinnamon to retail and grocery stores between Sept. 8, 2025, and June 28, 2026.
 That long sales window matters for households. A jar bought last fall or this spring could still be in the pantry, and holiday baking season is about to put cinnamon into more foods children eat. The company said no illnesses have been reported to date.
 A 110-Gram Jar Sold From Texas to Massachusetts
 The 14 states are Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia, and Wisconsin. The notice does not name retailers or cities.
 According to the notice, the problem surfaced after the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, a state-run research and testing laboratory, analyzed a sample and found elevated lead. The announcement does not give the amount of lead detected or say where the tested jar was bought.
 SLR said retailers should stop selling the product and hold remaining inventory. Consumers are told not to eat it and to throw it away or return it to the store for a full refund. Questions can go to the company at 1-516-437-3782, Monday through Friday, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. Eastern, or by email at slrusaorder@gmail.com.
 Not the First Wise Wife Cinnamon Pulled for Lead
 This is the second time in about 13 months that a Wise Wife ground cinnamon product has been recalled over lead. In September 2025, SLR recalled a smaller 50-gram jar with a different UPC, 0 688474 302853, after FDA testing found elevated lead. That jar was sold in New Jersey, New York, Florida, Maryland, Minnesota, Oklahoma, and Ohio from Feb. 15, 2024, to June 28, 2025, and the FDA now lists that recall as terminated.
 The FDA later added the earlier jar to its running public health alert on ground cinnamon , reporting a lead level of 2.49 parts per million. As of a Sept. 28 update, that alert lists more than 20 products from brands such as HAETAE, Roshni, Durra, BaiLiFeng, and Lior Gourmet Spices, with reported levels from about 2 ppm up to 10.7 ppm. The new 110-gram product did not appear on the list as of Nov. 1.
 Shoppers who checked for Wise Wife last year should look again, because the new jar has a different size, UPC, and date code. The two recalls overlap in New York, Minnesota, and Ohio.
 Both recalls are separate from the 2023 WanaBana apple cinnamon fruit pouch investigation, in which cinnamon used in the pouches contained lead at levels as high as 5,110 ppm, according to the FDA's investigation summary . The CDC's final count tied that event to 519 confirmed, probable, and suspected cases in 44 states, Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico. Nothing in the current notice links Wise Wife cinnamon to that investigation.
 Young Children Carry the Greatest Lead Risk
 The concern with lead in a pantry staple is repeated, low-level exposure over time, particularly for babies and toddlers. "No safe blood lead level in children has been identified," the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says. The agency adds that even low levels have been shown to affect learning, attention, and academic achievement.
 The FDA has explained its focus on cinnamon in similar terms, noting in its alert that the spice "is used in many foods young children consume." The agency also says high exposure in the womb, in infancy, or in early childhood can cause neurological effects.
 The recall notice says short-term exposure to very low levels may cause no symptoms, and an elevated blood lead level may be the only sign. Children exposed over weeks to months can suffer permanent nervous system damage, learning disorders, developmental defects, and other long-term health problems.
 The CDC uses a blood lead reference value of 3.5 micrograms per deciliter to identify children with more lead in their blood than most U.S. kids. The number, adopted in October 2021, reflects the highest 2.5% of children ages 1 to 5. It is a screening benchmark rather than a safe limit.
 Checking the Pantry and Getting a Blood Test
 Because most children with lead in their blood show no obvious symptoms, a blood test is the only reliable way to know whether exposure occurred. Families who used the recalled cinnamon regularly, especially in food for young children or during pregnancy, can ask a pediatrician or primary care clinician whether testing makes sense.
 Cost may not be a major barrier for many families. Medicaid requires blood lead screening for enrolled children at 12 and 24 months, and some local health departments offer free or low-cost testing. Keeping a photo of the label can help clinicians track exposure.
 The recall also highlights a gap in federal standards. The FDA's Closer to Zero initiative aims to steadily reduce lead, arsenic, cadmium, and mercury in foods for babies and young children, and in January 2025, the agency issued final guidance setting action levels for lead in processed foods for babies and young children. That program does not set limits for spices, so cinnamon recalls still depend largely on testing by the FDA and state labs.
 Next, watch whether the FDA adds the 110-gram jar to its cinnamon alert and whether officials release retailer names or the lead level found. Until then, the practical step is simple: check any Wise Wife cinnamon at home, stop using a jar that matches, and talk with a clinician if a young child or pregnant person ate it often.

 Key Questions Answered
 Which cinnamon product is being recalled? Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon in a 110-gram (3.88-ounce) clear plastic jar with a black cap, UPC 0688474302754, and a Best Before date of 4/25/2027.
 Where and when was it sold? It went to retail and grocery stores in 14 states, including New York, Texas, Pennsylvania, Ohio, and Michigan, between Sept. 8, 2025, and June 28, 2026.
 Has anyone gotten sick? SLR Food Distribution said no illnesses have been reported to date.
 Is this the same Wise Wife cinnamon recalled in 2025? No. The 2025 recall involved a 50-gram jar with UPC 0 688474 302853. The new recall covers a larger 110-gram jar with a different UPC.
 How much lead was found? The recall notice does not state a level. The FDA reported 2.49 parts per million in the earlier 50-gram Wise Wife product.
 Should my child get a blood lead test? If a child ate food made with the recalled cinnamon regularly, ask a pediatrician. Most children with elevated lead have no obvious symptoms, so a blood test is the only way to know.
 What should I do with the jar? Do not eat it. Throw it away or return it to the store for a full refund, and contact SLR at 1-516-437-3782 with questions.
